session.question: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?
session.answer:
The context indicates that first-tier suppliers (FTs) do not merely transmit sustainability requirements verbatim to second-tier suppliers; instead, they interpret those requirements through their own judgment and then enact them as boundary-spanning actions. However, the available excerpt does not specify the detailed mechanisms of this interpretation. It only shows that FTs’ behavior varies along a spectrum from compliance-oriented actions, where they pass on and enforce requirements, to improvement-oriented actions, where they adapt requirements into more proactive supplier-development efforts. Their interpretation is shaped by the downstream relationship with the focal firm, especially the level of cognitive and relational social capital, which influences how strongly they identify with and understand the sustainability agenda. (jia2021theboundaryspanningrole chunk 1)

Thus, “personal interpretation” appears to mean that FTs exercise discretion in translating focal-firm sustainability demands into locally meaningful practices for second-tier suppliers. In practice, this may involve deciding whether a requirement should be treated as a minimum compliance issue or as an opportunity for capability improvement. The context further suggests that this interpretive role is important because FTs act as boundary-spanners between the focal firm and upstream suppliers, and their sensemaking mediates how sustainability initiatives are implemented in the supply chain. (jia2021theboundaryspanningrole chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-5ea822a4: The paper examines how first-tier suppliers act as boundary-spanners between a focal firm and second-tier suppliers when sustainability-oriented supplier development is extended upstream. It finds that downstream cognitive and relational social capital between the focal firm and the first-tier supplier influences whether the supplier uses compliance-oriented or improvement-oriented boundary-spanning actions with second-tier suppliers. A key insight is that first-tier suppliers often add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when carrying out this role. This makes the paper relevant to personal interpretation and sensemaking in implementing sustainability requirements, especially in boundary-spanning frontline roles.
From Meng Jia, Mark Stevenson, and Linda C. Hendry. The boundary-spanning role of first-tier suppliers in sustainability-oriented supplier development initiatives. International Journal of Operations & Production Management, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856, doi:10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856.

pqac-6061945f: The excerpt says the paper identifies that first-tier suppliers (FTs) sometimes add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when acting as boundary-spanners, but it does not explain exactly how they do so in detail. The abstract indicates this occurs in the upstream relationship with second-tier suppliers and is influenced by the cognitive and relational capital in the downstream relationship between the FT and the focal firm. It also distinguishes between compliance-oriented and improvement-oriented boundary-spanning actions, suggesting that personal interpretation may shape whether FTs simply pass on requirements or adapt them into more proactive improvement efforts.
From Meng Jia, Mark Stevenson, and Linda C. Hendry. The boundary-spanning role of first-tier suppliers in sustainability-oriented supplier development initiatives. International Journal of Operations & Production Management, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856, doi:10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856.

pqac-f6e9583d: The excerpt discusses green entrepreneurial orientation, boundary-spanning search, and enterprise sustainable performance, based on manufacturing SMEs. It finds that green entrepreneurial orientation positively affects economic, environmental, and social performance, and that boundary-spanning search fully mediates these effects. Boundary-spanning search is described as a way to obtain external knowledge and resources for coordinated sustainable development. Environmental dynamism strengthens the effects of boundary-spanning search on economic and environmental performance, but weakens its effect on social performance. The paper uses organizational search theory and dynamic capability theory.
From Ye Fang, Yi Yang, Haiyan Xia, Yixuan Shao, Xieguo Gu, and Jiaqiang Shen. Green entrepreneurial orientation, boundary-spanning search and enterprise sustainable performance: the moderating role of environmental dynamism. Frontiers in Psychology, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.978274, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2022.978274.

pqac-874dc28a: The excerpt is about a 2021 conceptual paper on supply chain managers’ cognitive frames and sustainable supply chain management. It explains that little is known about cognitive processes in SCM and proposes three ideal-type cognitive frames: unidimensional, hierarchical, and paradoxical. The paper argues that the frame a manager holds affects how sustainability-related supply decisions are made and discusses antecedents for these frames. It also emphasizes the boundary-spanning role of supply chain managers and notes implications for training future SCM professionals. However, it does not directly discuss frontline employees, personal interpretation, or sensemaking in implementing sustainability requirements.
From Lutz Preuss and Andrew Fearne. Cognitive frames held by supply chain managers: implications for the management of sustainability in supply chains. Supply Chain Management An International Journal, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/scm-08-2020-0364, doi:10.1108/scm-08-2020-0364.

pqac-863ed769: The excerpt describes a 2023 study on regional sustainable development in Ena City, Japan, using a Quadruple Helix framework. It focuses on knowledge-sharing among academia, industry, government, and civil society in a sustainability-oriented project. The findings note an initial gap between theoretical sustainability understanding and practical application, but the project enabled knowledge exchange across stakeholders. Roles identified include academics as bridging actors, industry as resource providers, government as observant, and civil society as boundary-spanning. The paper argues for a balanced QH model and bottom-up sustainability initiatives. It does not specifically discuss frontline employees, personal interpretation, or sensemaking.
From Muhammad Mohsin Hakeem, Hoe Chin Goi, Frendy Frendy, and Hiroshi Ito. Regional sustainable development using a quadruple helix approach in japan. Regional Studies Regional Science, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1080/21681376.2023.2171313, doi:10.1080/21681376.2023.2171313.

contexts.context: The excerpt is a 2024 PLoS ONE article on green sustainability in the hotel sector. It examines how corporate social responsibility (CSR) relates to employees’ energy-specific sustainable behavior (ESBE), with green intrinsic motivation and personal environmental norms as mediators. The paper emphasizes psychological underpinnings connecting CSR to sustainable employee behavior and suggests CSR initiatives aligned with employee values can promote sustainability in hospitality, supporting UN-SDGs. It does not mention personal interpretation, sensemaking, boundary spanning, or frontline employees explicitly.
